entity_resolution.arabic_name: أبو الريحان محمد بن أحمد البيروني
alternative_names: Abu Rayhan Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Biruni
entity_resolution.nationality_context: Khwarazmian / Iranian scholar of the Islamic Golden Age

importance_evaluation.scientific_significance: Pioneered empirical measurement in geodesy, mechanics, and hydrostatics. Developed a trigonometric method to determine the Earth's radius using mountain height and horizon dip angle, and constructed precise hydrostatic apparatus to measure specific gravities of metals and minerals.
importance_evaluation.historical_significance: One of the most versatile polymaths of medieval Islam; made fundamental contributions to geodesy, astronomy, mathematics, geography, Indology, and comparative religion.

timeline_a_biological.event: Born in Kath, the capital of the Afrighid dynasty of Khwarazm.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Recorded in biographical traditions and verified by astronomical horoscopes in his own writings.

timeline_a_biological.event: Fled Khwarazm due to political instability following the Ma'munid takeover; resided in Rayy.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Documented in his autobiographical accounts and correspondence.

timeline_a_biological.event: Joined the court of Qabus ibn Ma'ali in Gurgan, where he composed 'Al-Athar al-Baqiya'.
Taken to Ghazna by Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni; subsequently traveled extensively across northern India.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Historical accounts in Kitab al-Hind and Ghaznavid historical chronicles.
Historical sources cite 440 AH (1048 CE), though some late sources suggest up to 1050 or 1052 CE.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Observed solar meridian altitudes and lunar eclipses in Khwarazm, coordinating with Abu al-Wafa in Baghdad to determine longitudes.
Completed 'Al-Athar al-Baqiya 'an al-Qurun al-Khaliya' (The Remaining Signs of Past Centuries), a treatise on comparative chronology and calendars.
Calculated the circumference and radius of the Earth at Nandana fort (Punjab) using mountain height and dip-of-horizon trigonometry.
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: Detailed in Tahdid Nihayat al-Amakin and Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Completed 'Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi' (The Mas'udic Canon), a massive astronomical compendium dedicated to Sultan Mas'ud.
Authored 'Kitab al-Jamahir fi Ma'rifat al-Jawahir', detailing experimental hydrostatics and specific gravity values.
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: Primary manuscript on mineralogy and hydrostatics.

physics_analysis.contribution_name: Trigonometric Geodesy and Earth Radius Calculation
physics_analysis.historical_claim: Determined the radius of the Earth using a single mountain observation and the dip angle of the horizon, avoiding long flatland distance measurements.
physics_analysis.scientific_problem: Determining the radius of Earth efficiently without requiring laborious distance measurements over flat terrain as performed by earlier Abbasid astronomers.
physics_analysis.historical_hypothesis: The radius of the Earth can be derived geometrically if the height of a mountain and the angle of dip of the sea/horizon viewed from its peak are measured accurately.
physics_analysis.historical_model_or_framework: Spherical geometric model combined with local vertical triangle geometry.
physics_analysis.modern_interpretation: Calculates Earth's local radius $R$ via $R = \frac{h \cos\alpha}{1 - \cos\alpha}$. Values obtained were within ~0.5–1.0% of modern values depending on the cubit conversion.
physics_analysis.experiment_details: Measured mountain height $h$ using two-station baseline angle measurements. Climbed the mountain at Nandana, measured dip angle $\alpha$ using an astrolabe, and applied trigonometric ratios.

variables_definition.h: Height of the mountain above the surrounding flat terrain
variables_definition.\\alpha: Angle of depression (dip angle) of the horizon from the mountain peak

equations.validity_domain: Spherical Earth approximation; negligible terrain inclination variations.
equations.assumptions: Earth is a perfect sphere; atmospheric refraction angle is negligible or constant; observer horizon line is unobstructed flat plain.

physics_analysis.result_and_impact: Produced an Earth radius value equivalent to approximately 6,339 km ( modern value ~6,371 km). Established dip-angle geodesy as a standard method.
physics_analysis.limitations_and_boundary_conditions: Uncertainty in atmospheric refraction at low viewing angles; dependence on exact unit conversion of the medieval cubit (dhira').
physics_analysis.verification_note: Documented explicitly in Tahdid Nihayat al-Amakin with detailed mathematical derivation.

physics_analysis.historical_claim: Designed a custom conical hydrostatic vessel (pycnometer ancestor) to measure the relative density of metals and precious stones.
physics_analysis.scientific_problem: Measuring density and purity of materials without destructive analysis.
physics_analysis.historical_hypothesis: The weight of water displaced by a immersed solid object is directly proportional to the volume of the solid, enabling precise density ratios.
physics_analysis.historical_model_or_framework: Archimedean hydrostatics extended through empirical measurement of displaced liquid mass and volume.
physics_analysis.modern_interpretation: Empirical determination of specific gravity ($S.G. = \frac{m_{air}}{m_{air} - m_{water}}$). Al-Biruni noted temperature variations in water density.
physics_analysis.experiment_details: Built a conical vessel with a thin overflow spout near the top, weighed samples in air and water, and measured the weight/volume of displaced water.

Specific gravity (dimensionless density relative to water)
variables_definition.W_{\\text{air}}: Weight of the sample in air
variables_definition.W_{\\text{water}}: Apparent weight of the sample submerged in water

equations.assumptions: Constant temperature and fluid density during measurement; negligible surface tension effects at overflow spout.

physics_analysis.result_and_impact: Obtained specific gravity values for gold, mercury, copper, iron, and emeralds that match modern values within 1-2% accuracy.
physics_analysis.limitations_and_boundary_conditions: Surface tension effects at the overflow tube; thermal expansion of water (which al-Biruni explicitly noted across seasons).
physics_analysis.verification_note: Described in detail in Kitab al-Jamahir fi Ma'rifat al-Jawahir and later cited by Al-Khazini in Kitab Mizan al-Hikma.

collaborators: Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani (simultaneous eclipse observations for longitude calibration)

major_claims_audit.claim: Al-Biruni proved that the Earth rotates on its axis.
major_claims_audit.recommended_wording: Al-Biruni evaluated the hypothesis of Earth's diurnal axial rotation (discussing Al-Sijzi's astrolabe) and maintained that it was mathematically compatible with astronomical observations, though he considered physical proof inconclusive within Aristotelian physics.

major_claims_audit.claim: Al-Biruni calculated the Earth's radius with 99.7% accuracy.
major_claims_audit.recommended_wording: Al-Biruni calculated the radius of the Earth using a trigonometric dip-angle method; depending on the conversion used for the medieval cubit, his estimate is remarkably accurate within ~1% of modern values.
Al-Biruni exhibited a rigorous empirical methodology, systematic error checking, and experimental precision, contributing significantly to the development of early scientific methods.

major_uncertainties: Exact modern length equivalent of the Khwarazmian/Ghaznavid cubit used in his geodetic calculation.
Exact day of death in 1048 CE vs alternative minor historiographical traditions (up to 1052 CE).
high_risk_claims: Overclaiming heliocentrism or definitive advocacy of Earth's rotation rather than geometric equivalence.
Anachronistic modern terms applied to medieval experimental apparatus without historical context.
